newsitem.title: USA: "Jury rigging" threat in Gingrich probe - Democrats.
newsitem.headline: "Jury rigging" threat in Gingrich probe - Democrats.

text.p: Democrats sharply opposed Thursday any Republican changes in membership of the House Ethics Committee in the midst of a two-year investigation of House Speaker Newt Gingrich.

"Just as the American people are about to learn the truth about these ethics violations, the Republican leadership is trying to pick a new judge, rig the jury and undermine the investigation," Democratic Whip David Bonior of Michigan said.

Bonior spoke at a news conference after House Republican Leader Dick Armey announced that at Gingrich's request he had taken over the speaker's task of recommending appointees of the ethics panel to the party steering committee.
Bonior said current members "know this case inside out" and their replacement would lead to further delay.
Under a House rule limiting service on the ethics panel to six consecutive years, all but three of the panel's 10 members are due to be replaced in the new Congress starting Jan. 7.

The committee is due to issue its findings in the Gingrich case before then but if it finds reason to believe possible wrongdoing, the investigation would move into the next stage, which could include public hearings.
It is investigating alleged tax law and campaign violations and whether Gingrich had failed to provide accurate information to the committee.
In a statement, Armey said he hoped that a bipartisan way could be found to reconcile the term-limit rule "with the need to complete the committee's current work."

Referring to an ethics subcommittee handling the Gingrich investigation, the statement added: "Obviously, the four members of the investigative subcommittee should continue their work until they come to a resolution."

Under committee rules, any charges made against Gingrich by the investigative subcommittee would be adjudicated by the six other members of the full committee, acting in effect as a jury. A finding of guilt could result in punishment ranging from expulsion to loss or limitation of privileges.
Bonior, Gingrich's chief critic on ethics issues, appeared with other Democrats to denounce Armey's statement that he said left the door open to replacing other members of the committee.

Of the six members who would serve as adjudicators, three Republicans and one Democrat have completed their six-year terms. The Democrat, Jim McDermott of Washington, says he does not want to leave the committee now.
A Republican member, David Hobson of Ohio, said Thursday: "I'm not asking to stay on the committee. My six years are up."
Committee Chairman Nancy Johnson, R-Connecticut, has not said whether she would be willing to stay on.
Comments on the investigation Thursday conflicted with the talk of cooperation and bipartisanship following the Nov. 5 elections.

Armey, in his statement, recalled he had said politics could be put aside next year to work on the nation's problems and expressed disappointent that some Democrats "would choose instead to continue the tactics of an ugly campaign season that most Americans had hoped was finally over."
